## Introduction

This analysis aims to identify whether different diversity indices have different statistical power to pick up diversity effects. For that, we will model diversity effects roughly in line with Hong & Page (2004) and the extension to smoothed landscapes proposed by Grim and colleagues (2019).

Specifically, we imagine that a team is tasked with finding the best solution to a problem - and then model that search for the best solution as exploring a hilly landscape where each point represents a possible outcome with a quality value. Each team member starts at a different spot on this landscape—here determined by a single attribute that shapes their perspective, such as their age. From their starting point, each member "climbs" to a nearby peak by always moving to a slightly better neighboring solution until no further improvement is possible. The team's overall performance is measured by the best peak that any member reaches. In this case, diversity means having team members start from varied positions, which increases the chance that at least one person finds a particularly high peak in the landscape. This is in line with models of informational diversity, and allows us to model outcome data - and then test whether different diversity indices give us different statistical power to pick up such an effect.

To produce realistic effect sizes (correlations around r ≈ 0.2), we add random noise to team performance. This noise represents all the other factors that affect team outcomes beyond diversity alone—such as individual skills, team resources, coordination quality, motivation, and task-specific knowledge. Without this noise, the simulation would produce unrealistically large diversity effects. The noise ratio was calibrated through diagnostic testing to achieve effect sizes consistent with meta-analytic findings on diversity-performance relationships.

## Simulation Setup

```{r}
#--- Simulation setup ---
## Generate landscape of a given length and smoothness
# The smooth_window parameter controls how "smooth" or "rugged" the landscape is:
# - Lower values (e.g., 1-2) create a more rugged landscape with many local peaks
# - Higher values (e.g., 5-7) create a smoother landscape with fewer, broader peaks
# In Hong & Page's model, smoother landscapes reduce the advantage of diversity
generate_landscape <- function(n, lower = 0, upper = 100, smooth_window = 3) {
  raw_points <- runif(n, min = lower, max = upper)
  smooth_points <- stats::filter(raw_points, rep(1/smooth_window, smooth_window), sides = 2)
  smooth_points[is.na(smooth_points)] <- raw_points[is.na(smooth_points)]
  as.numeric(smooth_points)
}

# Hill climbing: each agent moves to adjacent positions that improve their score
# until reaching a local maximum (peak)
hill_climb <- function(start, landscape) {
  if (start > length(landscape) || start < 1) stop("Starting position out of bounds.")
  pos <- start
  repeat {
    left_val <- if (pos > 1) landscape[pos - 1] else -Inf
    right_val <- if (pos < length(landscape)) landscape[pos + 1] else -Inf
    current <- landscape[pos]
    if (left_val <= current && right_val <= current) break
    pos <- if (left_val >= right_val) pos - 1 else pos + 1
  }
  landscape[pos]
}

# Team performance is the best peak found by any team member
team_hill_climb <- function(team_starts, landscape) {
  peaks <- sapply(team_starts, function(start) hill_climb(start, landscape))
  max(peaks)
}

# Generate teams with varying diversity levels
# Uses a mixture approach: sample between uniform distribution (high diversity)
# and narrow range (low diversity) with mixing probability from beta distribution
generate_team <- function(size, n_teams, alpha = 2, beta = 5) {
  ages <- seq(25, 65, by = 1)
  p_diversity <- rbeta(n_teams, alpha, beta)
  teams_list <- vector("list", n_teams)

  for (i in seq_len(n_teams)) {
    p <- p_diversity[i]
    prob_narrow <- p
    prob_uniform <- 1 - p
    mean_age <- sample(30:60, 1)
    narrow_range <- (mean_age - 5):(mean_age + 5)
    narrow_range <- narrow_range[narrow_range >= 25 & narrow_range <= 65]
    probs <- rep(prob_uniform / length(ages), length(ages))
    narrow_idx <- match(narrow_range, ages)
    probs[narrow_idx] <- probs[narrow_idx] + prob_narrow / length(narrow_range)
    probs <- probs / sum(probs)
    team_ages <- sample(ages, size = size, replace = TRUE, prob = probs)
    teams_list[[i]] <- tibble(team_id = paste0("Team_", size, "_", i),
                              age = team_ages,
                              team_size = size)
  }
  dplyr::bind_rows(teams_list)
}

# Helper function to parse comma-separated string into numeric vector
parse_members <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(unlist(strsplit(x, ",\\s*")))
}

#--- A helper function to run one "condition" (factorial cell) ---
# Simulation function that returns detailed team scores
# noise_factor: Controls the amount of random noise added to team performance.
#              This represents other factors affecting performance beyond diversity
#              (e.g., skills, resources, coordination, motivation). Higher values
#              produce more realistic (smaller) effect sizes.
run_simulation <- function(team_size, smooth_window, n_teams = 250, n_landscapes = 250,
                          noise_factor = 1, teams = NULL) {
    if (is.null(teams)) {
    teams <- generate_team(team_size, n_teams)
  }
  
  # Calculate diversity metrics per team
  team_data <- compute_CEI(teams$age, group = teams$team_id,
                           range = c(min(teams$age), max(teams$age)),
                           return_df = TRUE) %>%
    rename(CEI = index_value) %>%
    left_join(
      teams %>%
        group_by(team_id) %>%
        summarise(
          Rao_Simpson_5 = compute_Rao(age, bins = seq(25, 65, by = 5)),
          Rao_Simpson_10 = compute_Rao(age, bins = seq(25, 65, by = 10)),
          Blau_5 = compute_Blau(age, bins = seq(25, 65, by = 5)),
          Blau_10 = compute_Blau(age, bins = seq(25, 65, by = 10)),
          CV = compute_cv(age),
          SD = compute_sd(age),
          .groups = "drop"
        ),
      by = c("group" = "team_id")
    )
  
  # Simulate landscapes and team performance
  landscapes <- map(1:n_landscapes, ~generate_landscape(n = 50, smooth_window = smooth_window))
  peaks <- tibble(id = 1:(nrow(team_data) * length(landscapes)),
                  team = NA_character_,
                  result = NA_real_,
                  landscape_id = NA_integer_)
  i <- 1
  for (landscape_idx in seq_along(landscapes)) {
    landscape <- landscapes[[landscape_idx]]
    landscape_sd <- sd(landscape)  # For noise scaling

    for (team in team_data$group) {
      team_members <- (team_data %>%
                         filter(group == team) %>%
                         pull(group_members) %>%
                         parse_members()) - 20
      # Get raw peak from hill climbing
      peak_raw <- team_hill_climb(team_members, landscape)

      # Add noise to represent other factors affecting team performance
      # (skills, resources, coordination, motivation, task-specific knowledge, etc.)
      peak <- peak_raw + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = landscape_sd * noise_factor)

      peaks[i, ] <- list(i, team, peak, landscape_idx)
      i <- i + 1
    }
  }
  
  # Scale performance (result) per landscape
  peaks <- peaks %>% 
    group_by(landscape_id) %>% 
    mutate(result = scale(result, center = FALSE)) %>% 
    ungroup()
  
  # Merge team diversity details
  peaks_joined <- peaks %>% 
    left_join(team_data, by = c("team" = "group"))
  
  peaks_joined
}

```

## Verify team generation produces full diversity range

Before running the full simulation, let's verify that our team generation approach creates teams spanning the full range from minimal to maximal diversity:

```{r diagnostic-diversity, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
# Generate a sample of teams to check diversity distribution
set.seed(123)
diagnostic_teams <- generate_team(size = 5, n_teams = 1000)

# Calculate CEI for diagnostic purposes
diagnostic_diversity <- diagnostic_teams %>%
  group_by(team_id) %>%
  summarise(
    CEI = compute_CEI(age, range = c(min(diagnostic_teams$age),
                                     max(diagnostic_teams$age))),
    min_age = min(age),
    max_age = max(age),
    range_span = max_age - min_age,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot distribution of diversity scores
p1 <- ggplot(diagnostic_diversity, aes(x = CEI)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of CEI across generated teams",
       subtitle = paste0("Range: ", round(min(diagnostic_diversity$CEI), 3),
                        " to ", round(max(diagnostic_diversity$CEI), 3)),
       x = "Coverage & Evenness Index (CEI)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# Plot range span distribution
p2 <- ggplot(diagnostic_diversity, aes(x = range_span)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "coral", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of age ranges",
       x = "Age range (max - min)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)

# Summary statistics
cat("CEI Summary:\n")
print(summary(diagnostic_diversity$CEI))
cat("\nAge Range Summary:\n")
print(summary(diagnostic_diversity$range_span))
```

The diagnostic plots confirm that our team generation produces a good spread of diversity levels, from very homogeneous teams (low CEI, narrow age range) to highly diverse teams (high CEI, wide age range).

## Run simulations

The simulation systematically varies team size (5 vs 10) and landscape smoothness (3 vs 5) in a 2×2 factorial design. Each condition is replicated across multiple landscapes explored by multiple teams.

**Note on computation time:** The simulation below runs 250,000 total iterations (1,000 teams × 250 landscapes × 1 run per team-landscape combination, across 4 conditions). With parallel processing, this takes approximately 15-20 minutes on a modern multi-core machine. Results are cached, so re-knitting the vignette will be much faster.

```{r run-simulation, cache=TRUE}
set.seed(1234)
# Simulation parameters
total_teams <- 1000        # Number of teams per condition
total_landscapes <- 250    # Number of landscapes per condition
chunks <- 25               # Split landscapes into chunks for progress tracking

# Pre-generate teams for each condition combination (teams are generated once per condition)
pre_generated_teams <- expand.grid(
  team_size = c(5, 10),
  smooth_window = c(3, 5)
) %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(teams = purrr::map(team_size, ~ generate_team(.x, total_teams)))

# Define factorial conditions and replications (chunks)
conditions <- expand.grid(
  team_size = c(5, 10),
  smooth_window = c(3, 5)
) %>%
  slice(rep(1:n(), each = chunks)) %>%
  mutate(chunk = rep(1:chunks, times = nrow(expand.grid(team_size = c(5, 10), smooth_window = c(3, 5))))) %>%
  left_join(pre_generated_teams, by = c("team_size", "smooth_window"))

# Run simulations in parallel over conditions, passing pre-generated teams into run_simulation
results <- with_progress({
  p <- progressr::progressor(steps = nrow(conditions))
  furrr::future_pmap_dfr(
    conditions,
    function(team_size, smooth_window, chunk, teams) {
      sim_data <- run_simulation(team_size, smooth_window, 
                                 n_teams = total_teams, 
                                 n_landscapes = ceiling(total_landscapes/chunks),
                                 teams = teams)
      p()  # update progress after each simulation run
      sim_data %>% 
        dplyr::mutate(team_size = team_size,
                      smooth_window = smooth_window,
                      chunk = chunk)
    },
    .options = furrr::furrr_options(seed = TRUE)
  )
})

# Save results for later use
# write_rds(results, "power_simulation_results.rds")
# To load: results <- read_rds("power_simulation_results.rds")

```

## Estimating the effects

We estimate effect sizes and power using a **realistic study design** where each team's performance is averaged across approximately 10 different tasks or measurement occasions. This approach:

1. Averages each team's performance across ~10 landscapes (within each chunk)
2. Computes the correlation between diversity and performance across the 1,000 teams
3. Summarizes these correlations across the 25 independent replications (chunks)

This design matches realistic empirical studies where team performance is assessed across multiple tasks or occasions to reduce measurement error, while avoiding the unrealistic extreme of averaging across hundreds of scenarios.

```{r}
# Helper functions to avoid power calculation errors when correlations are ~0
safe_required_n <- function(r, power_target = 0.9) {
  purrr::map_dbl(r, function(r_val) {
    if (is.na(r_val) || abs(r_val) < 1e-6) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }
    tryCatch(
      pwr::pwr.r.test(r = abs(r_val), power = power_target)$n,
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    )
  })
}

safe_power <- function(r, n) {
  purrr::map2_dbl(r, n, function(r_val, n_val) {
    if (is.na(r_val) || abs(r_val) < 1e-6) {
      return(NA_real_)
    }
    tryCatch(
      pwr::pwr.r.test(r = abs(r_val), n = n_val)$power,
      error = function(e) NA_real_
    )
  })
}

# Aggregate team-level performance (average across ~10 landscapes within each chunk)
# Each chunk represents one independent study replication
team_summary <- results %>%
  group_by(team_size, smooth_window, chunk, team) %>%
  summarize(result_mean = mean(result),
            CEI = first(CEI),
            Rao_Simpson_5 = first(Rao_Simpson_5),
            Rao_Simpson_10 = first(Rao_Simpson_10),
            Blau_5 = first(Blau_5),
            Blau_10 = first(Blau_10),
            CV = first(CV),
            SD = first(SD),
            .groups = "drop")

# Pivot diversity metrics to long format
team_long <- team_summary %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(CEI, Rao_Simpson_5, Rao_Simpson_10, Blau_5, Blau_10, CV, SD),
               names_to = "metric", values_to = "value")

# Compute the correlation (effect size) for each replication (chunk), condition, and metric
replication_corr <- team_long %>%
  group_by(team_size, smooth_window, chunk, metric) %>%
  summarize(correlation = cor(result_mean, value, use = "complete.obs"),
            .groups = "drop") %>%
  # Compute required N for both power targets
  mutate(
    n_req_80 = safe_required_n(correlation, power_target = 0.80),
    n_req_90 = safe_required_n(correlation, power_target = 0.90)
  )

# Aggregate across replications: mean effect size, its SE, and required sample sizes with CIs
summary_corr <- replication_corr %>%
  group_by(team_size, smooth_window, metric) %>%
  summarize(
    mean_r = mean(correlation),
    se_r = sd(correlation) / sqrt(n()),
    # Summaries for 80% power
    mean_n_req_80 = mean(n_req_80, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_n_req_80 = sd(n_req_80, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(n_req_80))),
    lower_n_req_80 = mean_n_req_80 - 1.96 * se_n_req_80,
    upper_n_req_80 = mean_n_req_80 + 1.96 * se_n_req_80,
    # Summaries for 90% power
    mean_n_req_90 = mean(n_req_90, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_n_req_90 = sd(n_req_90, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(n_req_90))),
    lower_n_req_90 = mean_n_req_90 - 1.96 * se_n_req_90,
    upper_n_req_90 = mean_n_req_90 + 1.96 * se_n_req_90,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

summary_corr
```

Let's create a clear summary table showing effect sizes and required sample sizes:

```{r summary-table}
# Create a comprehensive summary table
summary_table <- summary_corr %>%
  mutate(
    Condition = paste0("Team size ", team_size, ", Smoothness ", smooth_window),
    `Effect Size (r)` = sprintf("%.3f (SE = %.3f)", mean_r, se_r),
    `N for 80% power` = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f-%.0f)",
                                mean_n_req_80,
                                pmax(1, lower_n_req_80),
                                upper_n_req_80),
    `N for 90% power` = sprintf("%.0f (%.0f-%.0f)",
                                mean_n_req_90,
                                pmax(1, lower_n_req_90),
                                upper_n_req_90)
  ) %>%
  select(Condition, Metric = metric, `Effect Size (r)`,
         `N for 80% power`, `N for 90% power`)

knitr::kable(summary_table,
             caption = "Effect sizes and required sample sizes by metric and condition")
```

Now let's calculate specific statistics for the paper, including comparisons at the median meta-analytic sample size (N=103):

```{r paper-statistics}
# Calculate power at N=103 for each metric and condition
power_at_103 <- summary_corr %>%
  mutate(power_at_103 = safe_power(mean_r, n = 103)) %>%
  arrange(team_size, smooth_window, desc(power_at_103))

# Print results
cat("Statistical Power at N=103 (median from meta-analysis):\n")
cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n\n")

for (ts in unique(power_at_103$team_size)) {
  for (sw in unique(power_at_103$smooth_window)) {
    condition_data <- power_at_103 %>%
      filter(team_size == ts, smooth_window == sw) %>%
      arrange(desc(power_at_103))

    cat(sprintf("\nTeam size %d, Landscape smoothness %d:\n", ts, sw))
    for (i in 1:nrow(condition_data)) {
      cat(sprintf("  %15s: Power = %.1f%%, N for 80%% power = %.0f\n",
                  condition_data$metric[i],
                  condition_data$power_at_103[i] * 100,
                  condition_data$mean_n_req_80[i]))
    }
  }
}

# Calculate CEI advantage
cat("\n\nCEI Statistical Power Advantage:\n")
cat(strrep("=", 60), "\n")

cei_comparison <- power_at_103 %>%
  group_by(team_size, smooth_window) %>%
  summarise(
    CEI_power = power_at_103[metric == "CEI"],
    CEI_n_req_80 = mean_n_req_80[metric == "CEI"],
    CV_power = power_at_103[metric == "CV"],
    CV_n_req_80 = mean_n_req_80[metric == "CV"],
    Blau5_power = power_at_103[metric == "Blau_5"],
    Blau5_n_req_80 = mean_n_req_80[metric == "Blau_5"],
    .groups = "drop"
  )

for (i in 1:nrow(cei_comparison)) {
  cat(sprintf("\nTeam size %d, Smoothness %d:\n",
              cei_comparison$team_size[i],
              cei_comparison$smooth_window[i]))
  cat(sprintf("  CEI requires N=%.0f vs CV N=%.0f (%.0f%% fewer teams)\n",
              cei_comparison$CEI_n_req_80[i],
              cei_comparison$CV_n_req_80[i],
              (1 - cei_comparison$CEI_n_req_80[i]/cei_comparison$CV_n_req_80[i]) * 100))
  cat(sprintf("  CEI requires N=%.0f vs Blau_5 N=%.0f (%.0f%% fewer teams)\n",
              cei_comparison$CEI_n_req_80[i],
              cei_comparison$Blau5_n_req_80[i],
              (1 - cei_comparison$CEI_n_req_80[i]/cei_comparison$Blau5_n_req_80[i]) * 100))
  cat(sprintf("  At N=103: CEI power=%.1f%% vs CV power=%.1f%% (%.1f pp higher)\n",
              cei_comparison$CEI_power[i] * 100,
              cei_comparison$CV_power[i] * 100,
              (cei_comparison$CEI_power[i] - cei_comparison$CV_power[i]) * 100))
}

# Calculate average advantage across conditions
avg_cei_advantage <- cei_comparison %>%
  summarise(
    avg_n_reduction_cv = mean(1 - CEI_n_req_80/CV_n_req_80, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    avg_n_reduction_blau = mean(1 - CEI_n_req_80/Blau5_n_req_80, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    avg_power_gain_cv = mean((CEI_power - CV_power) * 100, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

cat("\n\nAverage CEI Advantage Across All Conditions:\n")
cat(sprintf("  %.0f%% reduction in required sample size vs CV\n",
            avg_cei_advantage$avg_n_reduction_cv))
cat(sprintf("  %.0f%% reduction in required sample size vs Blau (5-year bins)\n",
            avg_cei_advantage$avg_n_reduction_blau))
cat(sprintf("  %.1f percentage point power gain vs CV at N=103\n",
            avg_cei_advantage$avg_power_gain_cv))
```

## Power curves

The following figure shows statistical power as a function of sample size for each diversity metric across the different simulation conditions.

```{r power-curves, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
corrs <- summary_corr %>% rename(effect_size = mean_r)

# Extended range to show full power curves
n_range <- seq(20, 200, by = 5)

power_data <- corrs %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    n = list(n_range),
    power = list(vapply(n_range, function(n) safe_power(effect_size, n), numeric(1)))
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest(cols = c(n, power))

metric_colors <- c(
  "CEI"            = "#1b9e99",
  "Rao_Simpson_5"  = "#d95f02",
  "Rao_Simpson_10" = "#d95f02",
  "Blau_5"         = "#7570b3",
  "Blau_10"        = "#7570b3",
  "CV"             = "#22b93e",
  "SD"             = "#66a61e"
)



metric_linetypes <- c(
  "CEI"            = "solid",
  "Rao_Simpson_5"  = "21",
  "Rao_Simpson_10" = "31",
  "Blau_5"         = "22",
  "Blau_10"        = "32",
  "CV"             = "12",
  "SD"             = "2111"
)

power_data$metric <- factor(power_data$metric, levels = names(metric_colors)) %>%
  relevel("CEI") %>% fct_rev()

# Create better facet labels
power_data <- power_data %>%
  mutate(
    facet_label = paste0("Team size: ", team_size, "\nSmooth: ", smooth_window)
  )


ggplot(power_data, aes(x = n, y = power, color = metric, linetype = metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 103, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 103, y = 0.95, label = "N=103\n(meta-analysis\nmedian)",
           size = 3, hjust = -0.1, color = "grey40") +
  scale_color_manual(name = "Metric", values = metric_colors) +
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Metric", values = metric_linetypes) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2), labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by Sample Size and Diversity Metric",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows 80% power; dotted line shows median meta-analytic sample size",
    x = "Sample Size (Number of Teams)",
    y = "Statistical Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~facet_label, ncol = 2)
  


```

**Key observations from power curves:**

- Across all four conditions, the relative power of metrics shows consistent patterns
- At the median meta-analytic sample size (N=103), there are substantial differences in statistical power between metrics
- The power curves demonstrate how sample size requirements vary considerably depending on the choice of diversity metric

## Summary

This simulation study assessed the statistical power of different diversity indices to detect an effect of team diversity on performance, using an agent-based model inspired by Hong & Page (2004). Teams explored smoothed landscapes to find high-quality solutions, with diversity increasing the likelihood of finding better peaks.

**Key findings:**

1. **Effect sizes vary by metric**: The simulation revealed that different diversity metrics showed different correlation strengths with team performance, even though all captured the same underlying team compositions.

2. **Power differences are substantial**: At typical sample sizes used in team diversity research (median N=103 from meta-analysis), the choice of diversity metric substantially affects statistical power to detect the simulated diversity effect.

3. **Sample size requirements differ markedly**: To achieve 80% power, different metrics require substantially different sample sizes. The statistics generated above provide specific comparisons for each condition.

4. **Patterns are consistent across conditions**: The relative performance of metrics was consistent across different team sizes (5 vs 10) and landscape smoothness levels (3 vs 5), suggesting the findings are robust to these contextual factors.

**Implications for research:**

- The choice of diversity measure has important practical consequences for statistical power in team diversity research
- Researchers should consider the statistical properties of diversity measures alongside their conceptual fit
- Using measures with better statistical properties can reduce the risk of false negatives (Type II errors) in diversity research

**Limitations:**

- The simulation omits team dynamics, using the best individual solution as the team outcome
- The model represents only one mechanism by which diversity might affect outcomes (variety in starting positions)
- Real-world diversity effects may operate through different mechanisms not captured here
- The noise added to produce realistic effect sizes is generic and may not capture the specific sources of variation in real team settings

The code for this simulation is available in this vignette and can be adapted to explore other scenarios or diversity mechanisms. Researchers are encouraged to modify parameters to match their specific research contexts.
